# Exam 002: TCP congestion control
- Date: 2026-11-15
- Status: closed
- Conditions: closed-book; text

## Ticket
1. Core (1. The congestion window and the ACK clock: what limits how much a sender has in flight): A sender's congestion window stays at 100 segments of 1,448 bytes. The round-trip time is 80 ms, the slowest link on the path carries 100 Mbit/s, the receiver's window is far larger than the congestion window, the application always has data ready, and nothing is lost. Work out the throughput of this connection, showing why it is that value and not 100 Mbit/s.
2. Foundations (6. BBR: how a model-based algorithm differs, its trade-offs and fairness): A bulk transfer lasting several minutes uses Linux's BBR (version 1) over a path on which no packet is lost. Its throughput graph falls to almost nothing for about 200 ms roughly once every 10 seconds, then returns at once to the previous level. Explain why the algorithm needs to do this.
3. Transfer (9. Reading the evidence: ss and tcp_info fields, retransmit counters, packet captures): Your service is sending a 2 GB export to a client over a path that can carry 1 Gbit/s, and the transfer runs at about 6 Mbit/s. On the sending host, `ss -ti` shows the following for the connection. Determine from this output what is holding the transfer at that rate.

       State  Recv-Q  Send-Q   Local Address:Port    Peer Address:Port
       ESTAB  0       2905160  10.0.3.17:8443        203.0.113.50:51324
            ts sack cubic rto:288 rtt:85.3/1.2 mss:1448 pmtu:1500 rcvmss:536 advmss:1448 cwnd:90 bytes_sent:152999625 bytes_acked:152934465 segs_out:105665 segs_in:52840 data_segs_out:105663 send 12.2Mbps lastsnd:4 lastrcv:204000 lastack:4 pacing_rate 24.4Mbps delivery_rate 6.1Mbps delivered:105618 busy:204000ms rwnd_limited:201300ms(98.7%) unacked:45 rcv_space:14600 rcv_ssthresh:64088 notsent:2840000 minrtt:84.9 snd_wnd:65535

## Defence

### Part 1

**First pass (learner):** The sender can only have one congestion window of data in flight per round trip, so the throughput is cwnd divided by RTT. That is 100 × 1,448 bytes = 144,800 bytes, or about 1.16 Mbit, per 80 ms, which gives roughly 14.5 Mbit/s. It is not 100 Mbit/s because the link speed is only a ceiling. The sender has to wait for ACKs before it can send more, so the window and the RTT set the rate, not the link.

**Examiner:** You said: "The sender has to wait for ACKs before it can send more." Why is that so?

**Learner:** Because the congestion window is a limit on how much unacknowledged data the sender may have in flight at once. Once 100 segments are out and not yet acknowledged, the window is full, and the sender is not allowed to send another segment until an ACK comes back and frees a slot. Each ACK takes about one round trip to return, so in every 80 ms the sender gets to send roughly one window's worth of data. With no loss and the window fixed at 100, that repeats every round trip.

**Examiner:** What happens if the slowest link on the path carries 10 Mbit/s instead of 100 Mbit/s, with everything else on the ticket unchanged?

**Learner:** Then the link becomes the limit, because the window would allow about 14.5 Mbit/s but the link can only carry 10 Mbit/s, so throughput would be 10 Mbit/s. The sender still puts 100 segments in flight, but the slow link can't drain them as fast as they arrive, so the extra ones sit in a queue at the router in front of that link. I think that means the ACKs come back more slowly and the measured RTT rises above 80 ms. If I work it backwards, 1.16 Mbit per round trip at 10 Mbit/s gives an RTT of about 116 ms, so roughly 36 ms of that would be queueing delay. In a real network I would expect the queue to overflow and drop packets eventually, but with the window fixed at 100 and nothing lost, I think it just settles there.

**Stop:** the examiner ended the part after two follow-ups; the learner answered both without stating a limit and without contradicting the first pass.

### Part 2

**First pass (learner):** I have not worked with BBR and only know it is a congestion control algorithm in Linux, so this is a guess. Since nothing is lost, it cannot be reacting to loss, so I assume the dip is deliberate and periodic: the algorithm backs off on a timer to test or re-measure something about the path, then goes back to its old rate. I don't know what it measures or why it needs to nearly stop to do it.

**Examiner:** You said the algorithm backs off "to test or re-measure something about the path". Take that one step further.

**Learner:** If I have to guess, it connects to what I just worked out in Part 1: when the sender has more in flight than the slowest link can drain, a queue builds and the RTT it measures includes queueing delay. So maybe BBR nearly stops sending so that any queue it has built empties, and then it can measure the real round-trip time of the path without its own traffic inflating it. That would fit with nothing being lost, since it would have no loss signal to tell it a queue is there. I don't know beyond this point. I can't say what it does with that measurement, or why the dip is about 200 ms every 10 seconds.

**Stop:** stated limit ("I don't know beyond this point"), after one follow-up. The first pass was presented as a guess and also ended at a stated limit ("I don't know what it measures or why it needs to nearly stop to do it"); the suggestion about the queue and the round-trip time appeared only after the follow-up.

### Part 3

**First pass (learner):** The cwnd is 90 segments. With an MSS of 1,448 and an RTT of about 85 ms, that works out to about 12.2 Mbit/s, which matches the `send 12.2Mbps` field, so the congestion window is very small for a 1 Gbit/s path. I also see `rwnd_limited:201300ms(98.7%)`, so I think the receiver is what is keeping the congestion window down at 90. The client is probably reading slowly, and CUBIC can't grow the window because of that. The Send-Q of 2.9 MB shows our application has plenty of data waiting, so the problem is not on our side. I am not sure why the actual rate is 6 Mbit/s and not the 12 Mbit/s the cwnd would allow.

**Examiner:** You said: "I think the receiver is what is keeping the congestion window down at 90." Why?

**Learner:** Thinking about it again, I mixed up two different windows there. `rwnd_limited` means the sender was held back by the receiver's advertised window, which is a separate limit from the congestion window. The receiver doesn't set cwnd at all; the sender may only have the smaller of the two in flight.

The output has `snd_wnd:65535`, which I take to be the receiver's advertised window in bytes. 65,535 / 1,448 is about 45 segments, and that matches `unacked:45`, so the sender only ever has 45 segments in flight, not the 90 that cwnd would allow. 65,535 bytes per 85.3 ms comes to about 6.1 Mbit/s, which matches `delivery_rate 6.1Mbps` and explains the gap between 6 and 12 that I couldn't account for in my first pass.

So I withdraw my statement: cwnd of 90 is not the binding limit, the receiver's 64 KB window is. cwnd probably stays at 90 only because the sender never fills it, so it has no reason to grow.

I don't know beyond this point why the client advertises only 65,535 bytes. My earlier guess was that the client application reads slowly, but I can't tell from this output whether that is the cause or something else is.

**Stop:** stated limit ("I don't know beyond this point why the client advertises only 65,535 bytes"), after one follow-up. In that answer the learner withdrew the first-pass statement that the receiver keeps the congestion window at 90, and settled the first-pass uncertainty about 6 Mbit/s versus 12 Mbit/s.

## Verdict

- Part 1: Holds. The first pass gave window / RTT = 144,800 bytes per 80 ms, about 14.5 Mbit/s, with the reason the link speed is not reached (the link is a ceiling; a full window admits a new segment only when an ACK returns, one round trip later). Under the two follow-ups the learner explained the window as a cap on unacknowledged data in flight, and for a 10 Mbit/s bottleneck gave 10 Mbit/s with a standing queue and an RTT of about 116 ms. Both agree with the answer key, and nothing in the first pass was withdrawn.
- Part 2: Fails at fundamentals: what BBR measures about the path, and why that measurement requires it to almost stop sending. The first pass was presented as a guess and ended with "I don't know what it measures or why it needs to nearly stop to do it", so the central point of the part was missing. The suggestion about the queue and the round-trip time came only after the follow-up, was offered as a guess, and ended at a stated limit ("I can't say what it does with that measurement") that lies inside what the Standard requires.
- Part 3: Edge found at telling the receiver's advertised window apart from the congestion window as the limit that binds, corrected under probing; and at the cause of an advertised window of exactly 65,535 bytes, a stated limit inside what the Standard requires. The first pass read the fields correctly, computed the 12.2 Mbit/s that the congestion window would allow, pointed to `rwnd_limited` and ruled out the sending application, but said the receiver "is keeping the congestion window down at 90" and left the gap between 6 and 12 Mbit/s unexplained. After one follow-up the learner withdrew that statement and gave the diagnosis of the answer key (`snd_wnd:65535`, 45 segments in flight, 6.1 Mbit/s).
- Overall: certifies that, closed-book and in text, the learner can derive a connection's throughput from its congestion window and round-trip time, explain why returning ACKs set that rate, and predict the result of a slower bottleneck link (area 1); does not certify the reason for BBR's periodic drain (area 6), nor reading `ss` output to name the binding window and the cause of a 65,535-byte receive window without correction (area 9), and this ticket did not touch areas 2, 3, 4, 5, 7, 8 and 10.

## Debrief notes

These notes are for the tutor.

### Part 1 (held)

No model answer is needed. For the record, the probing covered two of the points the answer key places within the Standard (why the sender must wait for ACKs; a slower bottleneck). It did not ask about a changed RTT, a larger window up to and beyond what the path holds (about 690 segments), a faster link, or a receive window smaller than the congestion window. These were not examined; nothing is known about them from this exam.

### Part 2 (failed at fundamentals): model answer

- BBR does not react to loss. It builds a model of the path from two measured quantities: the bottleneck's delivery rate (the maximum recently observed) and the round-trip time of the path with no queueing (the minimum recently observed). Their product is the amount of data that fills the path without a queue. BBR paces at about the measured rate and caps data in flight at a small multiple (2x) of that product.
- The minimum round-trip time can be observed only when the bottleneck queue is empty. A flow sending at or near the bottleneck rate keeps some queue there (its own and that of competing flows), so its ordinary samples are inflated. The two quantities cannot be measured well at the same time: measuring the rate needs the pipe full, measuring the base RTT needs it nearly empty.
- The estimate cannot be kept for ever, because the path can change (a route change raises the true RTT). The minimum is therefore taken over a window (10 seconds) and expires. If no sample at least as low arrives within that window, BBR deliberately stops filling the path: it cuts data in flight to a minimum (4 packets) for at least 200 ms and at least one round trip, so that the queue drains and a clean sample is taken. That is the dip. Throughput returns at once to the previous level because the rate estimate was kept.
- Why it is needed and not a nicety: with no loss signal, nothing else corrects an RTT estimate that is too high. Too high an estimate gives too large an in-flight cap, which gives a standing queue, which inflates further samples. The periodic drain breaks this loop.
- Within the Standard under probing: the cost, about 2 per cent of throughput (200 ms in 10 s) and a visible periodic stall that matters for latency-sensitive or steady-rate traffic.
- Also acceptable as an additional reason: fairness. The drain empties the queue, so competing BBR flows see the low RTT at the same moment, reset their timers together and drain together afterwards, which lets them converge on a shared, correct RTT estimate. Given alone, without the point that the flow's own traffic hides the base RTT, it is incomplete. Also correct: an application-limited or idle flow gets clean samples naturally and need not dip.
- Not acceptable: "it is reacting to congestion or loss", or "it is probing for more bandwidth" (the upward rate probe raises the rate and does not produce a near-zero dip).
- Not required: the exact constants, the name ProbeRTT, the gain cycle of the other phases, the kernel's filter, later BBR versions.

What the transcript shows: the learner stated at the outset that they had not worked with BBR. After the follow-up they reasoned from Part 1 to "nearly stop so the queue empties and the real round-trip time can be measured", as a guess, and stopped there. Missing: that BBR is model-based and what the two quantities are, what the RTT estimate is used for, why the estimate must expire, and why nothing else would correct it.

### Part 3 (edge): model answer

- Diagnosis: the transfer is receiver-limited. The peer's advertised receive window, not the congestion window, the network or the application, holds it at about 6 Mbit/s.
- Evidence:
  - `snd_wnd:65535`: the peer advertises 65,535 bytes. `unacked:45` x `mss:1448` = 65,160 bytes: data in flight is pinned at the largest whole number of segments that fits in that window.
  - `rwnd_limited:201300ms(98.7%)` of `busy:204000ms`: for almost the whole life of the connection the sender had data and was stopped by the receive window.
  - The rate follows: 65,535 bytes x 8 / 0.0853 s = 6.1 Mbit/s, which is the `delivery_rate`.
  - Not the congestion window: `cwnd:90` is twice what is in flight, and `send 12.2Mbps` is twice the delivery rate. The window is not being used up; the sender does not grow a window it is not using.
  - Not the application: `notsent:2840000` and a Send-Q of 2.9 MB show data waiting; `busy` equals the connection's lifetime.
  - Not loss or path congestion: no retransmission fields appear (`ss` prints `retrans`, `lost`, `bytes_retrans` only when non-zero), no `ssthresh` is shown, and `rtt:85.3` is within half a millisecond of `minrtt:84.9`, so no queue is building.
- The remedy lies on the receiving side; sender-side changes (congestion control algorithm, initial window, sender buffers) cannot help.
- Cause of a window of exactly 65,535 (within the Standard under probing), either of:
  - it is the largest value the 16-bit window field can carry without window scaling, so scaling was not negotiated on this connection (disabled on the client, or stripped by a middlebox or old load balancer); the option line `ts sack cubic` shows no `wscale` entry, which `ss` prints only when scaling is in use;
  - a receive buffer deliberately capped near 64 KB.
- Also acceptable: "the client application reads slowly" as a possibility, if the learner says what would distinguish it: a slow reader shows an advertised window that shrinks and fluctuates, sometimes to zero, not one fixed at the 16-bit maximum with steady delivery at exactly window / RTT. Also acceptable: naming the fix (enable window scaling, raise the client's receive buffer, or remove the middlebox), with the side effect that the congestion window and the path then become the limit and loss or queueing may appear.
- Not acceptable: "congestion-limited because cwnd is only 90", "application-limited", or "limited by the 85 ms RTT" with nothing said about which window binds.

What the transcript shows: the first pass merged the two windows ("the receiver is what is keeping the congestion window down at 90") and could not account for 6 against 12 Mbit/s. One open "Why?" was enough for a complete and correct repair, including the arithmetic for 45 segments and 6.1 Mbit/s and the outline reason `cwnd` stays at 90. This is recorded as corrected under probing. The learner then stated a limit at the cause of the 65,535-byte window and said the output could not tell them whether a slow reader was the cause. The exclusion of loss and path congestion and the side on which the remedy lies were not stated and were not asked.

### Agenda for the next learning session

1. BBR from the beginning (area 6): the two measured quantities and the model built from them; why the base RTT is hidden by the flow's own traffic; why the estimate expires; why no other signal corrects it when loss is ignored; the cost of the drain; fairness between BBR flows.
2. The two windows as separate limits (areas 1, 8, 9): the sender may have in flight the smaller of the congestion window and the advertised window; practise naming the binding one on a first reading of `ss -ti` output (`snd_wnd`, `unacked`, `rwnd_limited`, `cwnd`, `send` against `delivery_rate`), before computing anything.
3. Window scaling and the 16-bit window field (area 9): what 65,535 means, how the absence of `wscale` shows in `ss`, the other causes of a small fixed window, and how a slow reader looks different in the evidence.
4. Completing a diagnosis (areas 8, 9, 10): the evidence that rules out loss and path congestion (absent retransmission fields, no `ssthresh`, `rtt` against `minrtt`), on which side the remedy lies, and the side effects of the fix.
5. Area 1 beyond what was asked: the effect of changing RTT and window, the point where a larger window only builds a queue, and a receive window smaller than the congestion window. These were not probed in this exam.
